blocks.heading: Nationalisation and privatisation
blocks.text: Nationalisation transfers a privately owned business or industry into state ownership and control. Privatisation transfers a state-owned business or activity into private ownership and control. The directions are opposite: private to state, or state to private. A new owner may change objectives, investment and decisions, but a change in owner is distinct from a guaranteed improvement in performance. Nationalisation may protect essential service access but creates state financing demands. Privatisation may introduce commercial incentives, but service conditions may be needed to protect unprofitable users. A sale to investors within Namibia is still privatisation if state ownership transfers to private owners. Nationalisation does not mean selling abroad or banning imports; those concern international trade, not a transfer of ownership. Identify the enterprise whose ownership changes.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Assume a fictional state-owned coach company is sold entirely to private investors. In a separate event the state buys a privately owned water supplier. The coach sale is privatisation because ownership moves from state to private investors. The water purchase is nationalisation because it moves in the reverse direction. The buyers’ nationality does not determine either classification.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why selling shares to the public does not by itself nationalise a business. Assume all shares of fictional Hano Ltd remain owned by private investors, although anyone eligible can buy them.

Nationalisation transfers a privately owned enterprise into state ownership and control. Here private investors still own the shares, so it remains private sector. Public availability of shares concerns a company’s ownership form, whereas public-sector status concerns state ownership; the word public is being used in two different ways.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain whether either event is nationalisation: a Namibian state authority buys a privately owned local coach firm, while a different private firm begins selling cushions to Botswana.

The state purchase is nationalisation because control and ownership move from private owners to the state. Selling cushions across a border is exporting, a form of international trade. No ownership transfer is stated for the cushion business. Nationalisation is tested by the change of owner, not the country where products are sold.
